title: Spaghetti Bolognese
subtitle: The British home version: beef mince, tinned tomatoes, and dried pasta
excerpt: Britain's most-cooked midweek pasta: beef mince simmered with tinned tomatoes, onion, garlic, and herbs, served over dried spaghetti. Not an Italian ragu but a British family meal in its own right.
sourceNotes: Delia Smith, How to Cook (1998), spaghetti bolognese as a weeknight staple in British home cooking. Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management (1861), Project Gutenberg #10136, minced meat sauces for pasta. The British version developed independently of the Italian ragu bolognese and has its own established domestic tradition.

recipe.freezeNotes: The sauce freezes well for up to 3 months. Cool completely, then freeze in portions. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat gently.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the sauce and freeze half. Cook the pasta fresh each time.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The sauce keeps in the fridge for 3 days and improves overnight.

content.text: British spag bol bears no resemblance to an Italian ragu and is not trying to. It is a midweek meal: beef mince with tinned tomatoes, softened onion and garlic, dried herbs, and a long simmer to thicken the sauce. Served over spaghetti with grated cheddar or parmesan on top, it is one of the most reliably popular meals in British home cooking.

Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large frying pan over medium heat. Add {{onion}} finely diced onion, {{carrot}} finely diced carrot, and {{celery}} finely diced celery sticks. Cook, stirring regularly, for 8 to 10 minutes until soft and just beginning to colour.
Add {{garlic}} cloves of garlic and cook for 1 minute more. Push the vegetables to the side of the pan.
Raise the heat to medium-high. Add {{beef-mince}} of beef mince and break it up with a wooden spoon. Cook for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring regularly, until browned all over with no pink remaining.
Add {{tinned-tomatoes}} of tinned tomatoes, {{oregano-dried}} of dried oregano, and {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves. Add {{worcestershire-sauce}} of Worcestershire sauce if using. Season well.
Bring to a gentle simmer, then lower the heat and cook uncovered for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and the liquid has reduced.

About 15 minutes before the sauce is done, bring a large pan of heavily salted water to the boil. Cook {{pasta-dried}} of spaghetti according to the packet, minus 1 minute. Reserve a mug of pasta water before draining.
Remove the bay leaves from the sauce. Add the drained pasta and a splash of pasta water. Toss to coat and serve immediately.

rows.cause: Not simmered long enough or tinned tomatoes too juicy
rows.fix: Keep the sauce on a steady simmer with the lid off for at least 30 minutes. It needs time to reduce.

rows.cause: Pan not hot enough when the mince was added
rows.fix: The pan must be hot before the mince goes in. Break it up constantly with the spoon for the first few minutes.

rows.cause: Under-seasoned or not enough cooking time
rows.fix: Add more salt and let it cook for another 10 minutes. Worcestershire sauce adds depth without noticeably changing the flavour.

rows.cause: Sauce and pasta not combined quickly enough
rows.fix: Have warm bowls ready. Add the drained pasta straight to the sauce pan, toss quickly, and serve immediately.

content.text: Spaghetti bolognese arrived in British kitchens in the 1960s and 1970s through cookery writers like Robert Carrier and Delia Smith. The British version diverged from its Italian source almost immediately. It uses tinned tomatoes instead of small amounts of fresh, dried pasta instead of fresh tagliatelle, and often grated cheddar on top instead of parmesan. By now it has been made the same way in British homes for three generations and is entirely its own thing.
